headline: High-risk workspace overlap: Cline’s default write/network/tool access can amplify prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when paired with a prompt-only content source.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a content-writing prompt repository with no runtime isolation, while Cline reads workspace files and uses MCP/browser tools. A shared filesystem or copied prompt content can let attacker-controlled text influence Cline’s tool use. The pairwise bridge is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF prompt content from awesome-prompts is copied into a Cline workspace file or MCP-fed context
IF Cline treats file content as instructions during tool use
mitigations: Keep prompt repositories read-only in a separate folder
Disable MCP servers for untrusted prompt content
Require manual review before any tool action triggered by pasted prompts
Use a dedicated workspace with no shared files
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for prompt text

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-prompts itself shows no data classes touched and no egress, but Cline reads workspace files, runs browsers, and has broad network egress. If sensitive material is placed in the same workspace as prompt content, Cline can transmit it to model providers or MCP endpoints. The shared-workspace pathway is plausible from the profiles, so leakage is a medium default risk.
conditions: IF sensitive files are stored in the same VS Code workspace as Cline
IF Cline sends workspace content to a configured model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Separate sensitive files from the Cline workspace
Turn off MCP servers for sensitive projects
Use a local-only model provider for that workspace
Review browser targets before any page load
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data loss prevention

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-prompts is non-runnable and has no write surfaces, but Cline can write the filesystem, modify git state, and run multiple instances sharing state via filesystem. If the prompt repository is opened in the same workspace or copied into a writable repo, Cline can overwrite files or race with other instances. Because Cline’s defaults are explicitly mutable and shared-state based, the conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF awesome-prompts content is placed inside a writable git workspace
IF two Cline instances operate on the same workspace path
mitigations: Open the prompt repo read-only
Use one Cline instance per workspace
Pause auto-commit or git-edit workflows
Back up the workspace before edits
requires-engineering: add file-locking around shared workspaces

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-prompts is a prompt source, so its outputs can become inputs to Cline. Cline then acts on workspace and browser/tool outputs with approval-per-tool, but that does not verify the correctness of the prompt content itself. The pair can therefore propagate bad instructions into downstream actions, though the approval step limits blast radius below high.
conditions: IF Cline uses a prompt from awesome-prompts as an operational instruction source
IF the prompt is not independently verified before tool execution
mitigations: Treat repository prompts as examples only
Require a second reviewer for any prompt-derived action plan
Run a dry-run before shell or browser actions
Limit browser actions to non-sensitive sites
requires-engineering: add output verification gates before execution

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, EU PII, or regulated data class is identified in awesome-prompts, so compliance exposure is limited. Cline does handle model-provider API keys and workspace files, which can create policy issues if regulated data is introduced, but that is not evidenced here. The other agent is not cited for residency because it touches no regulated data class.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the Cline workspace
IF the configured model provider or MCP server has stricter residency or retention rules than the workspace owner expects
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the workspace
Use a provider with documented residency controls
Review retention settings before use
Store API keys in a separate secret manager
requires-engineering: implement data-class routing by policy
